NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark for Multimodal Care-Pathway Reasoning in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma

Pengkai Wang Wei-Wei Zhang Yan Li Min Tang Zhitian Hou Zeyu Liu
Guanghao Zhu Yuanyi Wang Yanggan Gu Wenjun Wang Minheng Ni
Congkai Xie Zhijie Sang Jianmin Wu Ying Sun Hongxia Yang
The Hong Kong Polytechnic University infix.ai Sun Yat-sen University
Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center Monash University
 GitHub Code    Hugging Face Data ††thanks: Equal contribution.††thanks: Corresponding authors.
Abstract

Current medical benchmarks typically break down clinical competence into isolated factual questions, single-image tasks, or static case vignettes. These tests score individual answers, but reveal less about whether a model can integrate subspecialty knowledge with multimodal evidence and track a patient’s condition throughout a course of care. To close this gap, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC). NPCBench mirrors specialist training, from guideline and foundational knowledge to case planning, longitudinal review, CarePath integration, and open-ended consultation. It contains 4,777 component and consultation items and a 100-patient CarePath cohort with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks. The episode-level evaluation tests whether diagnostic and care answers are jointly correct within a care pathway. By linking stepwise tasks to patient-level care trajectories, NPCBench evaluates whether models ground decisions in visual evidence, interpret changes in patient state, and meet clinical requirements in consultation. Across 30 evaluated models, we observe a composition gap: strong performance on individual tasks does not ensure jointly correct diagnostic and care answers for the same patient. Among 21 multimodal models, strict CarePath success reaches at most 23%. Paired controls and physician calibration further examine evidence grounding, longitudinal revision, and consultation judging. Overall, NPCBench broadens the evaluation of medical artificial intelligence beyond static question-answering paradigms to an apprenticeship-oriented assessment of clinical workflows, thereby offering a testbed for evidence-based and temporally coherent reasoning in oncology care.

1 Introduction

Medical large language models (LLMs) and multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) now achieve strong results in medical examinations, visual question answering, and broad benchmark suites [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. However, exam-style accuracy offers limited insight into subspecialty care, where clinicians must synthesize disease-specific guidelines, multimodal evidence, and evolving patient states over time. During clinical apprenticeship, physicians do not learn these skills in isolation. Recalling a clinical guideline is only the first step; specialists must also ground staging in diagnostic images, tailor treatment plans to patient constraints, and revise decisions as new responses or toxicities emerge. Evaluating medical AI therefore requires following this same progression from foundational knowledge to longitudinal management. While isolated tasks can pinpoint weaknesses in individual skills, only linked patient episodes can reveal whether these skills succeed together for the same patient [7, 8, 9].

Evaluating the progression from individual competencies to integrated clinical care requires a disease setting in which multimodal evidence and sequential decisions are closely connected. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC), prevalent in Southern China and Southeast Asia [10, 11, 12], is managed according to staging systems and clinical guidelines [13, 14, 15]. Diagnosis, staging, and risk assessment require integrating histopathology, multi-sequence MRI, and plasma EBV DNA [16, 11]. Clinical evidence and management objectives vary across stages of care, with subsequent decisions shaped by both the current patient state and preceding clinical events. During treatment and follow-up, tumor response, treatment-related toxicities, and recurrence or progression may influence management strategies [14, 15, 12]. NPC therefore provides a suitable setting for evaluating both individual specialist competencies and their integration across successive stages of care.

To systematically assess these capabilities, we introduce NPCBench, a clinical apprenticeship benchmark for NPC modeled on the progressive training of specialist physicians. As shown in Fig. 1, it organizes the evaluation into six progressive levels and an open-ended consultation suite. L1 and L2 test guideline recall and application. L3 tests pathology and MRI evidence grounding. L4 tests case planning from a single patient state, L5 longitudinal decision revision, and L6 linked CarePath episodes. O1 evaluates rubric-based specialist consultation. By pairing component tasks with patient trajectories, NPCBench asks a central measurement question: Are diagnostic and care answers jointly correct for the same patient when component scores are high? Models with similar average accuracy can exhibit different patient-level error patterns, or even select the right treatment while misinterpreting the underlying MRI evidence. NPCBench therefore pairs task-level scores with strict patient-level correctness, while holding patients and questions fixed in matched controls to examine how visual evidence, clinical chronology, and answer formats shape model decisions.

Using NPCBench, we investigate four research questions (RQ1–RQ4) across 30 medical and general-purpose models. RQ1 examines how well models translate guideline knowledge into case-level planning: guideline recall exceeds 92%, whereas the highest case-planning accuracy is 71.9%. RQ2 probes whether staging predictions are grounded in accurate visual interpretation: complete invasion correctness reaches at most 5.0% on the 100-patient anatomical panel, showing that correct stage labels often lack complete anatomical support. RQ3 examines decision revision and patient-level success: history can correct answers and introduce new errors. In CarePath, Gemini-3.1 achieves 89.9% Care accuracy but 11.0% Strict success; Claude-4.6 has the highest Strict success at 23.0%. RQ4 assesses consultation safety and automated judge reliability: GPT-5.1, the highest-scoring consultation model, triggers major-error criteria in 14.6% of responses under the primary judge, while rubric judges show sensitivity–specificity imbalances against physician annotations.

We summarize the main contributions of this work as follows.

  1. ①

    A clinical apprenticeship evaluation framework. We shift the evaluation focus from static answer correctness to pathway correctness. NPCBench assesses whether models make consistent clinical decisions across patient-state transitions, integrating guideline constraints, multimodal evidence grounding, and longitudinal disease evolution.

  2. ②

    A specialist-curated multimodal and longitudinal dataset. We release 4,777 component and consultation items alongside 100 CarePath episodes with 417 scored diagnostic and care tasks, unifying guideline rules, pathology slides, multi-sequence MRI scans, longitudinal EHR trajectories, and consultation rubrics within a single oncology pathway.

  3. ③

    Diagnostic dissection of the clinical composition gap. Across 30 models, we combine capability profiling with controlled interventions and physician-calibrated judging to identify where visual grounding separates from treatment decisions, how patient history changes decisions, and where high local scores coexist with patient-level errors.

2 Related Work

From exam QA to clinically structured benchmarks. Early evaluations of medical LLMs relied on static, examination-style question–answering benchmarks, including MedQA [17], MedMCQA [18], PubMedQA [19], the medical subsets of MMLU [20], MultiMedQA [2], MedBench [21], CMB [22], and CMExam [23]. These benchmarks capture medical knowledge and local reasoning, but they do not test whether a model can accumulate patient evidence, review decisions, and preserve coherence across the care pathway. Recent broad suites such as MedHELM [8], MedXpertQA [24], and AnesSuite’s AnesBench [25] move the evaluation toward clinically meaningful capabilities and specialty-aware reasoning. NPCBench follows this direction and makes the clinical apprenticeship ladder explicit: it measures component skills alongside longitudinal decisions and episode-level care correctness.

Multimodal, longitudinal, and rubric-based clinical evaluation. Medical MLLM benchmarks have expanded from image QA datasets such as VQA-RAD [26], SLAKE [27], and PathVQA [28] to broader evaluations of multimodality, trustworthiness, endoscopy, clinical reasoning, and sequence grounding [29, 30, 31, 32, 33]. In parallel, HealthBench [34], LiveMedBench [35], LLMEval-Med [36], MedDialogRubrics [37], and ClinConsensus [38] use expert-validated rubrics or temporally grounded cases to evaluate open-ended clinical responses. Workflow-oriented resources such as MedJourney [39], MedAgentBench [40], MedAgentBoard [41], and MTBBench [42] further shift evaluation from static snapshots toward state transitions. NPCBench brings these directions into a single disease setting: pathology and MRI evidence grounding, patient-level longitudinal revision, strict CarePath episodes, and criterion-level consultation rubrics. Appendix B gives a fuller comparison with recent medical benchmark families.

3 NPCBench: A Clinical Apprenticeship Benchmark

3.1 Overview

NPCBench organizes the clinical apprenticeship framework into a progressive capability ladder (L1–L6) and cross-level consultation rubrics (O1). The ladder spans guideline memory, atomic application, multimodal evidence grounding, case-level planning, longitudinal decision revision, and linked care episodes. Lower levels (L1–L4) assess individual capability components; L5–L6 examine longitudinal decisions and joint diagnostic–care correctness within patients. O1 complements these tasks by assessing free-text consultation quality. These tasks assess whether specialist decisions follow guidelines, use multimodal evidence, and remain consistent with a patient’s clinical course.

Four design principles guide task construction and clinical review: (i) Competence isolation requires each level in the progressive capability ladder (L1–L6) to measure a distinct, clinically meaningful component of specialist competence. (ii) Evidence-boundary control fixes the available evidence at the intended clinical decision point, removing future treatment, outcomes, and other answer-leaking cues. (iii) Clinical determinacy requires reference decisions supported by guidelines or expert consensus, given the provided clinical evidence. (iv)Auditable open-ended scoring uses case-specific consultation rubrics (O1) to assess clinical justification, evidence grounding, conditional reasoning, and safety. All patient materials are de-identified, and NPC oncologists verified component validity, decision determinacy, and the fidelity of patient-state transitions. Figure 2 shows the composition of each subset, and Fig. 3 illustrates the pipeline for constructing L1–L5 items.

3.2 Construction and Validation

Expert-curated clinical materials are converted into standardized evaluation items and reference answers. L1–L2 were derived from CSCO and NCCN guidelines; L3 from pathology and multi-sequence MRI images; and L4–L6 and O1 from de-identified real-world patient records, covering case-level planning, longitudinal decision-making, full CarePath evaluation, and open-ended consultations with scoring rubrics.

Multidisciplinary reviewers in oncology, pathology, and radiology assessed clinical validity, evidence sufficiency, and reference standards. For L1–L2, experts verified guideline consistency and answer determinacy; for L3, they validated pathology labels, MRI sequence and anatomical structure identification, invasion status, and T/N staging against imaging evidence. For L4, they assessed case sufficiency and appropriateness of reference decisions given patient-specific clinical states; for L5–L6, they verified evidence from decision-points, reference actions, and transitions from clinical state; and for O1, they reviewed core clinical requirements, supporting evidence, conditional recommendations, and major/minor error criteria to ensure clinically valid and auditable scoring.

3.3 Evaluation Levels and Scoring Units

L1.G-Mem: Guideline memory. The 250 expert-reviewed questions assess NPC guideline knowledge: 153 have both CSCO and NCCN support, 80 CSCO support only, and 17 NCCN support only. They probe treatment indications, staging implications, recommendation boundaries, surveillance, and contraindications. Item accuracy is the primary endpoint.

L2.A-App: Atomic guideline application. The 185 short-vignette questions cover initial definitive management, recurrence, metastatic/systemic management, and toxicity or contraindications. The main score averages accuracy over these four capability groups, giving each group equal weight.

L3.MM-EG: Multimodal evidence grounding. Pathology contains 69 overview cases (39 NPC-positive and 30 negative). MRI comprises 200 sequence-recognition questions, 400 T-stage cases, and 400 N-stage cases, with patient-disjoint T and N cohorts. Within the 400 T-stage cases, a 100-patient anatomical panel provides 2,700 structure cards covering 18 base structures, evaluating both structure identification and tumor invasion assessment. Overall, we report pathology, MRI sequence, structure-identification, T-stage, and N-stage accuracy separately, with additional metrics for invasion accuracy, joint structure–invasion correctness, and evidence-grounded T-stage success.

L4.C-Plan: Case-level planning. The 165 questions cover 84 patient groups and provide clinical snapshots of stage, treatment history, response, organ function, and other relevant constraints. Plausible alternative plans test whether a model identifies the next action appropriate to that specific state. Patient-macro accuracy weights patients equally.

L5.L-Rev: Longitudinal revision. The 305 questions cover 100 trajectories with one to five scored checkpoints at treatment, reassessment, toxicity, recurrence, or follow-up. Each checkpoint requires interpreting new findings in the context of earlier treatment and response. We report turn-micro accuracy and all-turn patient success. The primary task supplies full history in one prompt; matched-history and serial-interaction controls are evaluated separately.

L6.CP-Epi: CarePath episodes. The 100-patient CarePath cohort comprises 417 tasks: 100 pathology assessments, 100 MRI T-stage assessments, and 217 care decisions. Clinical records remain patient-linked; care-decision selection uses model-informed difficulty enrichment to prioritize clinical decisions that challenge models (Appendix C.3.5). Strict requires correct pathology, MRI T-stage, and every care answer; structure predictions provide auxiliary diagnostics. Each care question is answered independently with clinical context, incorporating the model’s pathology/T predictions and reference N/M/overall stages where required.

O1.C-Rub: ConsultRubrics. The 103 consultation items span 42 patients and 1,726 rubric criteria: 1,069 positive requirements and 657 negative criteria. Satisfied positive requirements add weighted credit; triggered major and minor errors deduct two and one points, respectively. The sum is floored at zero after item-level aggregation, normalized to 0–100, and averaged over all 103 item scores. The primary judge and physician calibration are described below.

4 Experimental Evaluation

4.1 Experimental Setup

Evaluation Models. We evaluated 30 medical and general-purpose models, including HuatuoGPT-o1 [43], Lingshu [4], Qwen, GPT-OSS [44, 45], and models from the GPT and Gemini families [46, 47]. While all 30 models complete the text-based tasks (L1, L2, L4, L5 and O1), the 21 multimodal models also complete the image-grounded tasks L3 and L6 (full model inventory in Appendix C.1).

Evaluation protocol. All models follow standardized task templates and scoring rules, with model-specific image processing and generation settings detailed in Appendix C and full prompts in Appendix E. For O1 calibration, automated judges and physicians evaluate identical response sets within each panel. All locally hosted generators and judges run on four NVIDIA A800-SXM4-80GB GPUs.

Patient-level Metrics. On CarePath episodes, we report both decision-level accuracy (Care\mathrm{Care}) and strict patient-level success (Strict\mathrm{Strict}), which requires correct pathology, MRI T stage, and all selected care answers for the same patient. For a given model, let p=1,…,Pp=1,\ldots,P index patients and 𝒮p\mathcal{S}_{p} denote the nonempty set of scored care decisions for patient pp, with np=|𝒮p|n_{p}=|\mathcal{S}_{p}| and N=∑p=1PnpN=\sum_{p=1}^{P}n_{p}. Let cp​jc_{pj}, dpd_{p} and tp∈{0,1}t_{p}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether the care response jj, the pathological label, and the T-stage MRI label are correct, respectively. With PP patients and NN total decisions, the percentage endpoints are

Care=100N​∑p=1P∑j∈𝒮pcp​j,Strict=100P​∑p=1Pdp​tp​∏j∈𝒮pcp​j.\mathrm{Care}=\frac{100}{N}\sum_{p=1}^{P}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}_{p}}c_{pj},\qquad\mathrm{Strict}=\frac{100}{P}\sum_{p=1}^{P}d_{p}t_{p}\prod_{j\in\mathcal{S}_{p}}c_{pj}. (1)

Appendix C.2.1 defines the remaining task metrics and 95% confidence intervals, and Appendix C.5.1 details the consultation scoring.

4.2 Guideline Knowledge and Case Planning

Table 1 summarizes model performance across all benchmark tasks. Addressing RQ1, we examine how foundational guideline competence translates into case-level planning. Although Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview leads the guideline recall with 94.0% and the atomic application with 92.5%, its precision drops to 71.9% in L4, followed by Claude-Sonnet-4.6 and Gemini-2.5-Pro. In addition, models with nearly identical L1 and L2 scores—such as GPT-5.1 and DeepSeek-V3.1—diverge sharply on L4 planning (63.5 vs. 51.8%). Although these subsets differ in item composition and weighting, this divergence shows that multi-factor case planning must be evaluated directly rather than inferred from guideline accuracy. Furthermore, a paired comparison on 71 physician-audited L1 items reveals that even high guideline scores partly rely on multiple-choice cues: removing answer options while holding the target knowledge fixed lowers accuracy by 7.0 percentage points (pp) for Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview, 12.7 pp for GPT-4.1, and 15.5 pp for GPT-5.1 shown as in Figure. 7i.

4.3 Evidence Grounding and Longitudinal Revision

Stage accuracy and anatomical grounding reveal different weaknesses. For RQ2, we first assess whether models can assign report-derived T and N categories across separate 400-patient cohorts. The highest T-stage accuracy is 43.5% across 400 patients, compared to a baseline of 37.5% in the majority-class. N-stage accuracy reaches 42.8% across a separate 400 patients, whose N1 majority baseline is 40.0%. However, overall accuracy masks differences in performance across different stages: Qwen3.6-27B achieves the highest overall N accuracy of 42.8% but only 31.9% balanced accuracy, whereas Gemini-3.1 maintains consistent performance across stages. Thus the total stage accuracy alone can therefore obscure class-imbalance shortcuts, a pattern that persists across T-staging image formats (Table A11) and on an external 53-patient cohort from a second center (Table A12).

A 100-case anatomical panel tests whether stage predictions rest on valid visual evidence. Direct T-stage accuracy reaches 43.0%, yet complete 18-structure invasion and evidence-grounded T-stage success (requiring correct labels and final stage) both fall below 5.0% (Table A15; Fig. 7a). Correct stage labels thus frequently coexist with flawed anatomical assessments. To isolate this breakdown, we test a fixed staging rule across three evidence conditions (Fig. 7f): reference findings (Ref.), predicted invasion with known anatomy (Known), and fully predicted evidence (Pred.). With reference findings, both a deterministic rule and a fixed GPT-OSS-120B stager reach 99.0% accuracy (Tables A17 and A18), confirming that downstream staging logic is sound. However, the accuracy of Gemini-3.1 drops to 49.0% (Known) and 36.0% (Pred.). Even with correct anatomical localization, flawed invasion recognition remains the primary bottleneck. A separate 25-case static vs. cine MRI comparison yields an inconclusive T-stage difference (section C.4).

Longitudinal decision accuracy does not ensure patient-level success. For RQ3, we first examine L5 performance across 305 decisions from 100 patients. Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview achieves the highest turn accuracy (87.9%) and all-turn patient success (71.0%), followed by Claude-Sonnet-4.6 (85.2% and 63.0%, respectively; Fig. 4b). While turn accuracy measures individual decisions in isolation, all-turn success is substantially lower across models because it depends on how errors distribute across trajectories—any single misstep invalidates an entire patient episode.

In paired controlled runs across the same 305 questions and 100 patients, we compare full chronological history against a snapshot that strips time markers and regroups the same records by content (Table A25). Full history yields higher turn-accuracy point estimates for 14 of 20 models, yet the patient-bootstrap 95% confidence intervals span zero for 19 models; DeepSeek-V3.1 gains 4.9 pp and Gemini-3.1 gains 3.3 pp. Net gains can hide offsetting errors: GPT-5.1 is correct on 22 questions only with full history and 19 only with the snapshot. Thus a 1.0 pp turn-accuracy gain coexists with a 1.0 pp decline in all-turn success. Three of 20 models show opposite directions for these endpoints (Fig. 7b,g). Correcting one turn may leave other errors, whereas a new error can invalidate an otherwise correct episode.

To separate record order from temporal information, an order-only control shuffles complete lines while retaining all time markers. Nineteen of 20 models have confidence intervals spanning zero, with Gemini-3.1 as the sole exception (+3.0 pp; 95% CI: 0.6–5.7 pp). Tables A25 and A26 report the paired results. A separate conversation-retention comparison involving 87 patients also yields an interval spanning zero.

4.4 Consultation Quality and Physician Calibration

For RQ4, we assess whether consultations meet case requirements and avoid clinical errors. GPT-5.1 has the highest ConsultRubrics score with 58.4, although the primary GPT-OSS-120B judge identifies major and minor errors in 14.6% and 40.8% of its responses. Because sound clinical advice and unsafe recommendations frequently coexist within the same free-text answer, aggregate rubric scores must be interpreted alongside explicit error rates and topic breakdowns (Fig. 5a,c,d). Because the 103 consultations span 42 underlying cases, weighting the 42 cases equally rather than individual questions shifts model scores by only −2.0-2.0 to +0.1+0.1 points and leaves GPT-5.1 highest, as shown in Fig. 5b.

To assess judge reliability and sensitivity to calibration-sample composition, we conduct a Targeted Audit (548 criterion labels) and an Expanded Audit (1,013 labels from 54 responses across nine models on six cases; Table 2). GPT-OSS-120B achieves the highest agreement in the Targeted Audit (81.4%, κ=0.610\kappa=0.610), whereas Qwen3.6-27B leads the Expanded Audit (77.8%, κ=0.544\kappa=0.544), indicating differences in judge performance across calibration samples.

In the Expanded Audit, the primary GPT-OSS-120B judge agrees with physicians on 70.5% of criteria (case-resampled 95% CI: 66.2–77.7%), with 51.8% sensitivity and 85.8% specificity (Fig. A7). A positive label means that a criterion holds, including the presence of an error. Overlooking a satisfied requirement withholds credit, whereas overlooking an error avoids a deduction. Figure 7e shows recognition of physician-positive labels (sensitivity) and negative labels (specificity); panel j compares agreement by criterion type.

4.5 Integrating Evidence and Decisions within Patients

For RQ3, all-care correctness is Cp=∏j∈𝒮pcp​jC_{p}=\prod_{j\in\mathcal{S}_{p}}c_{pj} and joint pathology–MRI T-stage correctness is Fp=dp​tpF_{p}=d_{p}t_{p} (Eq. (1)). In the CarePath cohort, Gemini-3.1 achieves the highest Care accuracy (195/217 decisions, 89.9%) and All-care success (83.0%), yet its Strict success is only 11.0%. In contrast, Claude-4.6 achieves lower Care (80.6%) and All-care (64.0%) but the highest Strict success (23.0%; exact 95% CI: 15.2–32.5%; Fig. 4c–e). Thus care accuracy alone does not identify which models most often answer all diagnostic and care questions correctly for a patient.

Joint correctness identifies the patients behind this gap. For Gemini-3.1, 72 of 100 patients have all care decisions correct despite at least one incorrect pathology or MRI T-stage label; the corresponding number is 41 for Claude-4.6. Conversely, Hulu-Med-32B has 38 patients with both diagnostic labels correct but at least one incorrect care decision (Fig. 6; Table A20). Care answers and diagnostic labels can therefore disagree in correctness.

To further examine whether diagnostic evidence affects care decisions, we compare predicted and reference pathology, MRI T-stage, and invasion findings in 25 CarePath patients. Fourteen local models answer the same 146 care questions under both conditions, with other clinical context fixed. Patient-averaged care accuracy, excluding diagnostic scores, changes by −3.2-3.2 to +4.1+4.1 pp, with 12 of 14 intervals including zero (Fig. 7d; Table A23). These mixed changes show no consistent care benefit from reference evidence under the supplied clinical context.

Care and All-care outcomes also differ across episode groups. Nine of 21 models have lower decision-weighted Care but higher patient-weighted All-care in the 75 assigned-pathology episodes than in the 25 patient-matched episodes. Claude-4.6 scores 76.5% versus 84.3% for Care, but 68.0% versus 52.0% for All-care (Table A21). The groups contribute 102 and 115 decisions, respectively. Figure 7c,h further examines performance by decision count: 1–2/3/4–5 for L5 and 1/2/3–6 for CarePath, as patient-level success requires every scored decision to be correct.

Class imbalance also matters: constant T3 predictions score 58% in CarePath, above the best model’s 52%. The highest balanced T accuracy is 30.5%, versus 25% for constant predictions (Table A19; Fig. A4). L3 therefore complements CarePath’s joint endpoint with stage-discrimination and grounding tests.

5 Conclusion

NPCBench links foundational guideline knowledge and multimodal image interpretation to longitudinal decision-making, joint patient-level correctness, and specialist consultation in NPC care. Evaluating 30 models reveals that local accuracy rarely guarantees coherent patient management: stage predictions frequently lack complete anatomical support, longitudinal history corrects prior mistakes while introducing new errors, and high-scoring consultations still trigger critical safety violations. On CarePath episodes, accurate treatment choices routinely coexist with flawed image interpretations, capping strict patient-level success at just 23.0% despite substantially higher decision-level accuracy. These findings establish evidence–decision consistency as a central benchmark target: meaningful clinical progress requires models to ground interpretations in valid evidence and sustain accurate decisions across the entire course of care for the same patient.

Limitations. Our evaluation is constrained by primarily single-center records, assigned pathology in 75 model-selected CarePath episodes, score sensitivity to class balance and episode length, and the six-case Expanded Audit. Future more multi-center cohorts with fully patient-matched modalities and prospective studies are therefore needed to establish whether benchmark gains improve clinical care.

Appendix A Data Curation and Statistics

The following sections describe the clinical sources, question construction, patient coverage, and reference annotations.

Clinical data and ethics.

The retrospective use of clinical data was approved under IRB protocol B2026-465-01. Patient materials follow the hospital’s de-identification procedure. Direct identifiers and unnecessary location details are removed, and dates are expressed relative to the patient’s clinical course where appropriate. L4 retains clinical decision dates needed to identify the applicable guideline edition. Age and sex are retained when needed for reasoning. NPC oncology specialists review clinical validity, reference answers, supporting evidence, and transitions between care decisions.

Task construction.

L1 and L2 translate guideline knowledge and decision thresholds into questions with adjudicated answers. L4 combines diagnosis, stage, treatment history, response, toxicity, and patient-specific constraints into fixed-state planning cases. L5 organizes longitudinal records around clinical decision checkpoints, retaining the cumulative evidence available at each point and removing subsequent orders or outcomes that reveal the target decision. L6 links pathology, MRI, and selected care decisions within patient episodes. O1 uses consultation scenarios with separate criteria for core conclusions, supporting evidence, conditional reasoning, and clinically important errors. L1 retains item-level guideline references and supporting evidence. All 350 L2/L4 items include their construction sources and reviewed answer rationales. Source records distinguish the guideline edition stated in a question from references supporting its answer: the former is available to the model, whereas the latter explains the reference decision. Recorded edition constraints occur in two L2 and four L4 questions and are included in the model inputs; edition and section references are available for a subset of items.

Clinical review and answer format.

The evaluated sets contain 250 L1, 185 L2, and 165 L4 questions. Reviewers checked the evidence available at the decision point, the applicable guideline, and whether the options supported a determinate answer. L2 includes one explicit multiple-select item and L4 includes two; the other items are single choice. Multiple-select answers must match the complete reference set. The question specifies this requirement, and selecting only part of the set receives no credit. Reviewed rationales accompany all 350 L2/L4 items.

Construction examples.

Figure 3 shows shortened examples of the released task formats. The examples retain the answer labels and decision-relevant information; full inputs and reviewed rationales accompany the dataset.

Data and code availability.

De-identified benchmark inputs, multimodal assets, reference annotations, and supplementary control datasets are publicly available on Hugging Face; evaluation code and inference scripts are available on GitHub. The released tasks include the CarePath cohort with 100 patients and 217 scored care decisions. Author-owned code is licensed under MIT and original data and annotations under CC BY 4.0; third-party materials retain their own terms.

A.1 Task Scope and Composition

Evaluation cohorts.

The L6 cohort contains 100 patients and 417 scored tasks: 100 pathology assessments, 100 MRI T-stage assessments, and 217 care decisions. Image-evidence replacement and serial-interaction analyses use 146 care questions for 25 patients within this cohort, as described in section C.4. These analyses use a fixed 146-question set, while the main benchmark scores 217 selected care decisions across all 100 patients.

The L1 guideline-memory set covers CSCO-only, NCCN-only, and dual-source questions. Among the 250 L1 items, 153 are supported by both CSCO and NCCN sources, 80 are CSCO-only, and 17 are NCCN-only. The L2 atomic-application set is organized into four capability families: initial definitive management (84 items), post-treatment recurrence (30), metastatic/systemic management (44), and toxicity or contraindication management (27).

Task categories.

Figure 2 uses the four L2 scoring groups. O1 contains 43 treatment, 35 adverse-event, 11 diagnosis, 12 special-population, and two workup questions; the special-population group comprises four elderly and eight pediatric items. The figure and score breakdown therefore refer to the same item tags. The figure abbreviates recurrent/metastatic disease as Rec./met., recurrence as Recur., radiotherapy as RT, treatment as tx, progression as Progress., planning/execution as Plan/exec., metastatic disease as Metast., toxicity/supportive care as Tox./supp., and special populations as Special pop. EBV denotes Epstein–Barr virus; M0 denotes no distant metastasis.

The L4 case-level planning set covers initial treatment (16 items), disease progression (43), regimen switching (100), and toxicity management (6), with patient-level aggregation over 84 patients.

A.2 MRI Cohorts and Patient Coverage

The T-stage cohort contains 400 patients, with T1/T2/T3/T4 counts of 50/50/150/150. The patient-disjoint N-stage cohort contains 400 patients, with N0/N1/N2/N3 counts of 80/160/80/80. Both use eighth-edition report-derived staging labels. The T cohort includes 374 M0, 14 M1, and 12 patients with unspecified M status; all 400 N-stage patients are M0. The 100-patient anatomical panel is contained within the T-stage cohort. The 200 sequence-recognition patients overlap the T and N cohorts in 67 and 59 patients, respectively, giving 874 unique patients across the main L3 MRI tasks. Pathology is counted separately as 69 specimens. Patient coverage is calculated from the union of the linked MRI records.

T-stage examinations span March 2021 to June 2024, as do N-stage examinations. The external MRI examinations were acquired at Nanfang Hospital from January 2023 to December 2024. Fifty-three examinations have a definite report-derived T label for scoring; two without a definitive reference are excluded. The external class counts are 4/8/31/10 for T1/T2/T3/T4.

L2 contains 47 clinical source cases and 138 constructed scenarios. L4, L5, L6, and O1 contain 84, 100, 100, and 42 task-level patient records, respectively. These task-level counts include cross-task overlap and therefore do not define a unique benchmark-wide patient total. Clinical records used in the EHR tasks span 2008–2025; these are source-record dates, not a common follow-up interval.

Appendix B Detailed Related Work

Static medical QA and broad medical suites. Examination-style benchmarks such as MedQA, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, the medical subsets of MMLU, CMB, and CMExam have provided a practical basis for assessing medical knowledge and localized reasoning skills [17, 18, 19, 20, 22, 23]. MultiMedQA and MedBench extended this approach by combining multiple medical QA datasets and testing more general medical reasoning across them [2, 21]. More recent benchmarks—including MedHELM, MedXpertQA, and AnesSuite’s AnesBench—emphasize construct validity, specialty-specific reasoning, and clinical abilities alongside exam-style performance [8, 24, 25]. NPCBench focuses on NPC and reports component performance and joint patient correctness separately.

Multimodal medical evidence grounding. Medical MLLM evaluation has progressed beyond image-question datasets like VQA-RAD, SLAKE, and PathVQA toward benchmarks with broader modality coverage and greater clinical specialization [26, 27, 28]. Frameworks such as OmniMedVQA, GMAI-MMBench, BenchX, CARES, and BrainMD assess dimensions including the breadth of medical imaging modalities, model reliability, and cross-modality generalization [29, 48, 49, 33, 50]. More domain-specific benchmarks—EndoBench, DrVD-Bench, MedSG-Bench, MMOral, M3CoT-Bench, and MedThinkVQA—target fine-grained image understanding, temporal or sequence-level grounding, and reasoning across multiple images [30, 32, 31, 51, 52, 53]. NPCBench examines these components in NPC, where pathology underpins diagnosis, MRI anatomy delineates local spread, sequence recognition shapes image interpretation, and assessment of local invasion guides staging and treatment intensity.

Rubric-based and real-world clinical response evaluation. Open-ended clinical evaluation is increasingly grounded in explicit scoring rubrics and physician-validated criteria. HealthBench assesses multi-turn health-related dialogues using item-specific rubrics; LiveMedBench focuses on temporally separated clinical cases; LLMEval-Med incorporates physician adjudication combined with checklist-guided evaluation; MedDialogRubrics and ClinConsensus extend rubric-based assessment frameworks to consultation and longitudinal care scenarios [34, 35, 36, 37, 38]. O1 ConsultRubrics uses the same criterion-level approach for NPC consultation, in which positive requirements capture key clinical conclusions, supporting patient evidence, and conditions that change the recommendation, whereas negative criteria differentiate between major and minor safety-critical errors.

Workflow, longitudinal, and agentic clinical benchmarks. Workflow evaluations test information gathering, interaction, and decisions across multiple steps. MedJourney structures evaluation around the patient journey, whereas MedAgents, MDAgents, MedAgentsBench, and MedAgentBoard focus on collaborative problem-solving, tool integration, and multi-step clinical task execution [39, 54, 55, 56, 41]. In oncology, MTBBench emulates multidisciplinary tumor-board decision-making, and recent work on autonomous oncology agents investigates specialized workflows for treatment decision support [42, 57]. AgentClinic evaluates tool use and information gathering in simulated clinical encounters, while MedAgentBench tests tasks in a FHIR-compatible electronic health record [58, 40]. Clinical-environment simulators additionally expose models to explicit state transitions [59]. NPCBench evaluates related questions within NPC: L5 tests decisions under different representations of longitudinal records, and L6 checks image labels and selected care answers for the same patient. Its primary care evaluation supplies clinical context without feeding previous care answers back, whereas separate serial controls test conversation retention. This distinction separates joint patient correctness from autonomous interaction with a clinical environment.

Appendix C Evaluation Protocol and Additional Results

The protocol specifies each task’s inputs, model interface, and scoring rule. L1/L2/L4/L5 use closed-choice answers; L3 uses diagnostic labels and structured image findings; L6 combines pathology and T-stage labels with care decisions; and O1 uses criterion-level judgments of free-text consultations. Table A6 summarizes the inputs and scoring populations for the linked and matched analyses.

Computing resources and generation settings.

Local experiments used institutional NVIDIA A800-SXM4-80GB servers with up to eight GPUs; the multimodal experiments also used a four-GPU server. The local environment used CUDA 12.8, PyTorch 2.10.0, vLLM 0.19.1, Transformers 5.6.2, and Accelerate 1.13.0. Models were run through vLLM or model-specific multimodal interfaces, with parallelism selected according to model size. Task-specific settings specify the model interface, image processing, sampling parameters, and output limits. CarePath evaluation uses maximum output lengths of 1,024 tokens for local models and 8,192 for API models. Missing or incomplete final answers receive zero credit.

For L5 primary and paired history evaluations, GPT-OSS-20B allows 16,384 output tokens and HealthGPT-Pro-4B 32,768. Fleming-R1-7B allows up to 16,384 within its 32,768-token context; each matched history/snapshot/shuffled triplet uses the same output allowance.

O1 uses output limits of 2,048 tokens for the 23 local generators and 16,384 tokens for the seven API generators. Its primary judge uses temperature 0 and top-pp 1, with a 2,048-token output limit and an 8,192-token retry for incomplete criterion judgments. All 30 models have valid judgments for all 1,726 criteria. The released evaluation code specifies the per-model settings.

Answer extraction.

Closed-answer tasks use a common final-answer rule. An explicit final boxed or labelled answer takes precedence over options discussed in intermediate reasoning; a standalone option is accepted when unambiguous. Missing or conflicting final answers are scored incorrect. Multimodal tasks extract the requested diagnostic and anatomical fields. O1 averages all 103 item-level rubric scores for every model.

MRI inputs and generation.

T staging uses two image presentations: 100 patients have 27 structure-centred cards per patient, and 300 have ordered groups of physically matched MRI planes. N staging uses the latter presentation for all 400 patients. Within an axial group, T1, T2, and enhanced T1 images are stacked vertically; a coronal group pairs enhanced fat-suppressed T1 with precontrast non-fat-suppressed T1. Each slice retains a 512×512512\times 512 display tile. Axial and coronal groups are 512×1644512\times 1644 and 512×1096512\times 1096 lossless PNGs, respectively. A request contains one patient’s ordered groups, with 44–79 groups per case. The T range extends from the suprasellar cistern to inferior C3; the N range extends from the skull base to the inferior sternoclavicular joint. Clinicians reviewed the selected anatomical coverage and report labels.

Qwen, Lingshu, HealthGPT, and Hulu-Med-4B use a 128,000-token context and an 8,192-token output budget for the plane-group tasks. Hulu-Med-4B uses spatial merge 2 with a 98,304 visual-token budget; Hulu-Med-7B/32B use merge 4, a 22,000 visual-token budget, and their 32,768-token context. Hulu images enter the processor as height–width–channel arrays. InternVL3.5 uses its 40,960-token context, dynamic cropping with at most four patches per group, and 33–35 uniformly sampled groups. Sampling allocates images proportionally between axial and coronal groups and retains both endpoints of each group.

API inputs preserve the same plane-group pixels: GPT-5.1 uses lossless WebP and the other services use lossless PNG. GPT-5.1 uses snapshot gpt-5.1-2025-11-13 with reasoning effort set to none. GPT-4.1 receives at most 50 groups, sampled proportionally within each anatomical group with both endpoints retained; the other API models receive all groups. Output limits are 4,096 tokens for GPT-4.1 and Claude, 8,192 for GPT-5.1 and Gemini Flash, and 16,384 for Gemini Pro. Empty Claude answers are retried at most three times; incomplete structured answers use 8,192 output tokens. Answers outside the requested categories are scored incorrect. Table A11 separates T accuracy by presentation, so the combined score can be interpreted alongside its two constituent cohorts. CarePath cohort uses its own ten-page MRI input and ninth-edition prompt.

C.1 Evaluation Models

Table A7 lists all 30 evaluated models. The nine text-only models cover the five text-based subsets; the 21 image-capable models additionally complete pathology, MRI, and CarePath evaluation. The inventory spans medical and general-purpose models, with local inference for open-weight models and API access for hosted services. The four models used in the CarePath cohort construction are marked throughout the results.

C.2 Task Definitions and Scoring

C.2.1 Notation and Aggregation

All definitions apply to one evaluated model on one stated cohort; the model index is suppressed. An indicator 𝟏​{E}\mathbf{1}\{E\} equals one if statement EE is true and zero otherwise. A sum counts contributions, a product of binary indicators requires every factor to be one, and |𝒜||\mathcal{A}| denotes the number of elements in a finite set 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

Missing or conflicting extracted answers have correctness zero and remain in the scored denominator. The six L6 treatment questions excluded for insufficient decision evidence are omitted from 𝒮p\mathcal{S}_{p} for every model. The CarePath cohort has P=100P=100 and N=217N=217. The image-label analysis uses 146 care questions for 25 patients within this cohort.

For closed-answer tasks, the item-micro accuracy and group-macro accuracy are

Accmicro=100n​∑i∈ℐai,Accgroup=100G​∑g=1G1|ℐg|​∑i∈ℐgai.\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{micro}}=\frac{100}{n}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}a_{i},\qquad\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{group}}=\frac{100}{G}\sum_{g=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{g}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{g}}a_{i}. (A1)

Here the GG nonempty, disjoint sets ℐg\mathcal{I}_{g} partition ℐ\mathcal{I}. Micro accuracy weights each scored item equally; group macro weights each group equally. L2 uses G=4G=4 clinical capability groups. For patient aggregation, let ℐp\mathcal{I}_{p} contain the scored items belonging to patient pp in the task being evaluated:

Accpatient=100P​∑p=1P∑i∈ℐpai|ℐp|,AllCorrect=100P​∑p=1P∏i∈ℐpai.\mathrm{Acc}_{\mathrm{patient}}=\frac{100}{P}\sum_{p=1}^{P}\frac{\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{p}}a_{i}}{|\mathcal{I}_{p}|},\qquad\mathrm{AllCorrect}=\frac{100}{P}\sum_{p=1}^{P}\prod_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{p}}a_{i}. (A2)

Each ℐp\mathcal{I}_{p} is nonempty. L4 reports patient-macro accuracy over 84 patients; L5 reports turn-micro accuracy and AllCorrect as all-turn success over 100 patients. For L6, ℐp=𝒮p\mathcal{I}_{p}=\mathcal{S}_{p} and ai=cp​ja_{i}=c_{pj} under the corresponding node indexing; AllCorrect is called AllCare. Its primary Care and Strict endpoints follow Eq. (1); AllCare omits the pathology and T-stage requirements.

Patient intersections.

Let 𝒞={p:Cp=1}\mathcal{C}=\{p:C_{p}=1\} and ℱ={p:Fp=1}\mathcal{F}=\{p:F_{p}=1\} be patient sets, and let superscript cc denote a complement within {1,…,P}\{1,\ldots,P\}. Table A20 reports set cardinalities. Equivalently, the four counts are

na​b=∑p=1P𝟏​{Cp=a,Fp=b},a,b∈{0,1},∑a=01∑b=01na​b=P.n_{ab}=\sum_{p=1}^{P}\mathbf{1}\{C_{p}=a,\ F_{p}=b\},\quad a,b\in\{0,1\},\qquad\sum_{a=0}^{1}\sum_{b=0}^{1}n_{ab}=P. (A3)

Thus n11=|𝒞∩ℱ|n_{11}=|\mathcal{C}\cap\mathcal{F}|, n10=|𝒞∩ℱc|n_{10}=|\mathcal{C}\cap\mathcal{F}^{c}|, n01=|𝒞c∩ℱ|n_{01}=|\mathcal{C}^{c}\cap\mathcal{F}|, and n00=|𝒞c∩ℱc|n_{00}=|\mathcal{C}^{c}\cap\mathcal{F}^{c}|. Strict is 100​n11/P100n_{11}/P; AllCare is 100​(n11+n10)/P100(n_{11}+n_{10})/P. All four groups refer to the same patients.

C.2.2 Classification Diagnostics

For a target class kk, TPk\mathrm{TP}_{k} counts correctly predicted members of that class, FNk\mathrm{FN}_{k} counts missed members, and FPk\mathrm{FP}_{k} counts other examples predicted as class kk. Class recall RkR_{k}, precision QkQ_{k}, and secondary F​1kF1_{k} are proportions:

Rk=TPkTPk+FNk,Qk=TPkTPk+FPk,F​1k=2​T​Pk2​T​Pk+FPk+FNk.R_{k}=\frac{\mathrm{TP}_{k}}{\mathrm{TP}_{k}+\mathrm{FN}_{k}},\qquad Q_{k}=\frac{\mathrm{TP}_{k}}{\mathrm{TP}_{k}+\mathrm{FP}_{k}},\qquad F1_{k}=\frac{2\mathrm{TP}_{k}}{2\mathrm{TP}_{k}+\mathrm{FP}_{k}+\mathrm{FN}_{k}}. (A4)

These ratios require nonzero denominators; undefined diagnostic ratios are unavailable. For KK evaluated classes with reference support, balanced accuracy is 100​K−1​∑k=1KRk100K^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{K}R_{k}. T staging uses K=4K=4 (T1–T4), so a majority-class predictor has 25% balanced accuracy. Per-class recalls shown as percentages equal 100​Rk100R_{k}. L3 structure-card accuracy and these class-balanced measures have different aggregation units; the main structure column uses card-micro accuracy.

C.2.3 Paired Effects and Uncertainty

For the binary endpoint in Eq. (A6), index the MM matched units by ii. Let ai(0)a_{i}^{(0)} and ai(1)a_{i}^{(1)} be correctness under baseline and intervention, respectively. The counts are u=∑i𝟏​{ai(0)=0,ai(1)=1}u=\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}\{a_{i}^{(0)}=0,a_{i}^{(1)}=1\} and v=∑i𝟏​{ai(0)=1,ai(1)=0}v=\sum_{i}\mathbf{1}\{a_{i}^{(0)}=1,a_{i}^{(1)}=0\}. The remaining M−u−vM-u-v units retain the same correctness. Consequently, Δ∈[−100,100]\Delta\in[-100,100] is a percentage-point difference and Φ∈[0,100]\Phi\in[0,100] is a percentage of correctness flips; changes between two incorrect answers do not contribute to either count.

The image-label comparison instead compares within-patient care accuracies. For condition k∈{0,1}k\in\{0,1\}, define the proportion Ap(k)=np−1​∑j∈𝒮pcp​j(k)A_{p}^{(k)}=n_{p}^{-1}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{S}_{p}}c_{pj}^{(k)}. With k=0k=0 for predicted image labels and k=1k=1 for reference image labels, its reported effect is

Δpatient=100P​∑p=1P(Ap(1)−Ap(0)).\Delta_{\mathrm{patient}}=\frac{100}{P}\sum_{p=1}^{P}\left(A_{p}^{(1)}-A_{p}^{(0)}\right). (A5)

Here P=25P=25 and ∑pnp=146\sum_{p}n_{p}=146. The better, worse, and same columns in Table A23 count patients according to the sign of Ap(1)−Ap(0)A_{p}^{(1)}-A_{p}^{(0)}. The patient-macro effect also incorporates each patient’s change in accuracy.

Confidence intervals.

Care accuracy and paired patient comparisons use a patient-cluster bootstrap. Each draw resamples patients with replacement, retaining all of a sampled patient’s scored units and both conditions of a pair. Each draw recomputes the relevant estimator: a ratio of turn totals for micro accuracy or a mean of patient accuracies for patient macro. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles form the reported 95% interval. L1 controls resample paired items; physician-calibration intervals resample consultation-response clusters. CarePath cohort strict-success intervals are exact binomial (Clopper–Pearson) intervals over 100 patients. Multi-model intervals are descriptive and unadjusted.

C.3 Extended Results and Diagnostic Analyses

The family profiles in Fig. A1 show that high guideline scores coexist with low strict patient-level success across model groups. Figure A2 retains the differences between individual models. We then examine longitudinal decisions, anatomical evidence, staging, and patient-level outcomes before comparing controlled changes to the inputs.

C.3.1 L5 Longitudinal Revision Results

L5 reports turn accuracy and all-turn patient success because the two measures answer different questions. Turn accuracy counts correct next actions, whereas all-turn success requires every scored answer for one patient to be correct. All models use the same boxed single-letter answer interface. The 100 patients have 13/19/31/24/13 trajectories with 1/2/3/4/5 scored turns, respectively; the all-turn requirement therefore ranges from one answer to five. Table  reports both endpoints so that differences in individual decisions can be distinguished from differences in complete episodes.

C.3.2 MRI T and N Staging

Table A11 separates card-based and plane-group T results because patient composition and image representation differ. The combined T400 score weights all 400 patients equally; N-stage balanced accuracy weights N0–N3 equally. Predictions outside the requested categories count as incorrect.

Prediction counts distinguish single-category predictions from answers outside the allowed categories. On the 300 plane-group T cases, Qwen3-VL-8B/30B-A3B, Lingshu-32B, and HealthGPT-Pro-4B always predict T4 (115/300 correct), whereas Hulu-Med-7B always predicts T1 (35/300). All five have 25.0% balanced accuracy. On N400, only 46/400 Lingshu-7B answers use a valid category (11.5%), all N3; 15 are correct, and balanced accuracy is 4.7%.

Second-centre MRI assessment.

The Nanfang Hospital panel uses clinical T-stage references associated with 53 MRI examinations. Each examination provides ten four-row panels, sampling 30 positions per acquired sequence across the panels. All ten images enter one request with an eighth-edition T-only prompt. Table A12 reports accuracy, balanced accuracy, and per-stage recall. T3 accounts for 31 of 53 cases, giving a majority-class accuracy of 58.5%. Hulu-Med-4B reaches 60.4% accuracy but 28.1% balanced accuracy, whereas Qwen3.5-35B reaches 50.9% and 39.8%, respectively. The class-dependent ordering shows that higher overall accuracy can coincide with poorer recognition of less frequent stages. This panel evaluates MRI staging at a second centre.

C.3.3 L3 Multimodal Evidence-Grounding Diagnostics

The L3 diagnostics examine three linked questions: whether the marked anatomy is identified, whether its invasion status is correct, and whether the resulting evidence supports the T category. They use the 100-case anatomical panel, with 18 invasion labels and one T category per patient. Structure identification is scored over 2,700 cards covering 18 base structures; nasopharynx cards are excluded from this primary MRI scoring set. The text-stager experiment uses structured findings as input; the CarePath and cine inputs are described in sections C.3.5 and C.4.

Patient-level measures then distinguish partial evidence from complete evidence. Pt. Inv. averages invasion correctness over all 18 structures within each patient and then across patients. Complete Inv. requires all 18 labels to be correct; EG T additionally requires the correct final T stage. A model can therefore obtain a correct direct T label while failing complete evidence or EG T. Table A15 reports these endpoints together, and the ablations below examine which errors remain when anatomical identity or invasion labels are supplied by the reference.

The patient-level MRI comparison uses the same structured response fields for local and API models.

C.3.4 L3 MRI Staging Ablations

The staging comparisons examine two possible sources of error: extracting anatomical findings and assigning a stage from those findings. The deterministic rule and GPT-OSS-120B stager assign T categories from structured anatomical findings. When gold 18-structure evidence is supplied, the stager approaches the gold ceiling; when model-generated evidence is supplied, performance remains much lower. Under this fixed structured-evidence interface, the contrast locates a major performance gap in structure and invasion extraction. The class recalls in Table A16 show that several models recognize advanced T categories more often than early categories. For example, GPT-5.1 reaches 39.0 Direct T but 27.9 Balanced T because most correct cases are T4, whereas Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview has lower micro Direct T but the strongest class-balanced recall among the listed patient-staging runs.

The deterministic structure-only rule assigns T4 when cavernous sinus invasion is present; otherwise T3 when skull-base, pterygoid-base, upper-cervical, or paranasal-sinus structures are invaded; otherwise T2 when the parapharyngeal-space, medial/lateral pterygoid, or longus-capitis labels are positive; otherwise T1. Levator veli palatini and carotid sheath are not used for upstaging in this 18-structure rule. The 99.0 Gold Rule ceiling indicates that one gold T4 case depends on staging evidence outside the scored 18-base-structure set.

Direct T is the patient-level T-stage answer generated by the evaluated model from the L3 patient prompt. Rule-slot T applies the deterministic structure rule described above to the evidence used in each experiment. The LLM-slot experiment uses a separate set of model-generated evidence summaries as input to GPT-OSS-120B. Its Rule-slot column applies the deterministic rule to those same summaries; Table A17 uses the primary L3 responses. The gap between the 99.0 gold-evidence ceiling and model-evidence LLM-slot scores shows how much the same downstream stager depends on the quality of its structured input.

C.3.5 CarePath Evaluation and Cohort Composition

The CarePath cohort contains 100 patients, 811 clinical context entries, and 217 scored care decisions. Each model provides 100 pathology predictions, 100 MRI predictions, and 217 care answers. Table A19 reports component performance and patient-level outcomes; Table A20 gives their intersections. Figure A5 shows how requiring pathology, T stage, and care answers to be correct together narrows the set of successful patients.

Cohort selection and modality linkage.

HealthGPT-Pro-8B, Qwen3-VL-8B, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B, and Qwen3.5-27B participated in cohort and decision selection. They are marked in the results tables, and the other 17 models were not used in cohort construction. The 25 episodes with matched pathology contribute 115 decisions; the 75 with assigned specimens contribute 102. MRI and clinical records are patient-linked throughout. All assigned specimens are labelled NPC-positive; the corresponding episode records identify their specimen source.

Selection used the four construction models’ care answers with gold pathology and MRI evidence and reference history. Twenty-five patients with matched multimodal data were included. Among the other 86 reviewed patients, those with at least one construction-model error were ranked first by total errors across models and checkpoints, then by the number of checkpoints missed by at least two models, checkpoints missed by any model, maximum errors per checkpoint, and mean errors per checkpoint; a fixed source identifier broke remaining ties. The first 75 patients completed the CarePath cohort. Within these 100 patients, checkpoints answered correctly by all four models were removed from scoring. This procedure yields 217 scored decisions, including a 93-decision subset missed by at least two construction models. Selection therefore targets clinically relevant decisions that these models found difficult.

Question review and scoring depth.

Six treatment questions are excluded from scoring because the source records do not establish a unique treatment choice at the specified checkpoint. The identified issues include combining ordered and administered medicines and incomplete evidence of radiotherapy. Their exclusion reasons accompany the data, and all 100 patients remain in the scored cohort. The scored set contains 52/23/3/7/8/7 patients with 1/2/3/4/5/6 care decisions, respectively. The 75 assigned-specimen episodes contain no scored initial-treatment-selection question; those questions occur in the matched-pathology group.

Clinical inputs and endpoints.

Care prompts incorporate predicted pathology and T-stage labels where specified: 207 reference predicted pathology, and 133 retain supplied N/M/overall-stage information. Prior care answers are not supplied in the primary protocol. Strict success requires correct pathology, correct MRI T stage, and every selected care answer for a patient. Care accuracy weights the 217 decisions equally; all-care correctness and strict success weight the 100 patients equally. MRI structure predictions and the 811 clinical context entries support the evaluation but are not additional strict-success criteria.

C.4 Controlled Input Comparisons

Reference image-evidence comparison.

This experiment asks whether incorrect image-derived findings account for errors in care answers. Fourteen local models answer the same 146 care questions for 25 patients within the 100-patient CarePath cohort, using predicted or reference pathology, MRI T stage, and invaded structures. Supplied N/M and overall-stage fields remain fixed. These patients have patient-matched pathology, MRI, and clinical records and contribute 115 decisions to the main benchmark; the paired analysis uses its fixed 146-question set. Additional conditions replace pathology or MRI findings separately or vary the supplied history. Table A23 reports joint evidence replacement with clinical context held fixed, using mean within-patient care accuracy and 10,000 paired patient-bootstrap draws. The endpoint scores care answers alone, so replacing an incorrect image label raises the score only if a care answer also improves.

History representation and record order.

The history comparisons separate two changes that might affect a clinical decision: removing temporal markers and changing the order in which records are presented. The snapshot removes relative-day and admission markers, then groups the historical records by content. Baseline and current findings, the question, options, and reference answer remain unchanged. Although the records match once temporal markers are ignored, their clinical timing is no longer explicit; this contrast combines loss of timing with reorganization. The order-only condition instead shuffles complete lines within their original sections, retaining every time marker.

Twenty models each answer the same 305 questions for 100 patients in all three conditions. These controls use condition-matched generations, with a full-history baseline evaluated alongside each altered representation. Full-history minus snapshot accuracy is positive for 14 models; only DeepSeek-V3.1 has a patient-bootstrap interval wholly above zero (Table A25). In the order-only comparison, 19 intervals include zero, while Gemini-3.1 improves by 3.0 pp (95% CI: 0.6–5.7; Table A26). Both analyses use 10,000 paired patient-bootstrap draws, with intervals unadjusted across models. Figure A6 places the full-history comparison alongside the image-evidence comparison, showing both the direction and uncertainty of each paired difference.

The history-dependent subset contains 118 turns from 69 patients and compares full history with current-state information alone (Table A24). A separate Gemini-3.1 experiment evaluates packed-history, persistent, and stateless interaction on 292 turns from 87 patients. Persistent and stateless turn accuracy are 82.5% and 83.6%, a difference of −1.0-1.0 pp (95% CI: −3.8-3.8 to 1.7). The interval includes zero.

Paired decision changes.

Across MM matched turns, let uu count incorrect-to-correct changes and vv correct-to-incorrect changes. Net accuracy change Δ\Delta in percentage points and correctness-flip rate Φ\Phi in percent are

Δ=100​u−vM,Φ=100​u+vM.\Delta=100\,\frac{u-v}{M},\qquad\Phi=100\,\frac{u+v}{M}. (A6)

For the full-history versus snapshot L5 comparison, M=305M=305 and each condition covers the same 100 patients. All-turn gain is the difference between the two conditions’ proportions of patients with every scored turn correct; it is not derived from uu and vv alone.

For L1, MRI T staging, and L5, a changed unit switches between correct and incorrect across the paired conditions. For the 25-case L6 control, a changed patient has different within-patient care accuracy. These counts capture offsetting improvements and regressions. GPT-5.1 changes correctness on 41 of 305 L5 turns (22 corrected, 19 regressed), with a net gain of 1.0 pp and an all-turn success change of −1.0-1.0 pp. Under gold pathology and MRI evidence, HealthGPT-8B improves care accuracy for eight patients and worsens it for ten; the remaining seven are unchanged. The L6 net difference averages the magnitudes of the within-patient accuracy changes.

A three-condition input example.

The accompanying example provides one complete L5 prompt triplet and its record correspondence. Each prompt has the same 46 historical records; 44 carry relative-day or admission markers in the full-history version. Table A27 shows two translated treatment-record excerpts. Drug names, doses, cycle number, and treatment intent are preserved, whereas the snapshot omits the admission/day prefix. The shuffled condition keeps each complete source line and changes its position. Baseline/current findings and all answer options remain identical. Removing the time markers changes the temporal information available for the decision.

Success at different scoring depths.

Figure 7c groups L5 patients by 1–2, 3, and 4–5 scored turns (n=32,31,37n=32,31,37); panel h groups CarePath cohort patients by 1, 2, and 3–6 scored care decisions (n=52,23,25n=52,23,25). For each model and group, success is the number of patients meeting the endpoint divided by the group’s patient count: all-turn correctness for L5 and strict success for the CarePath cohort. The groups differ in both clinical composition and the number of decisions required for complete success.

Serial CarePath interaction.

The 25-case serial control uses gold pathology and MRI evidence. For GPT-4.1, GPT-5.1, and Gemini-3.1, persistent-minus-stateless all-care correctness differences are 16, 20, and 8 pp, with paired 95% intervals of [−4-4,36], [−4-4,44], and [0,20], respectively. These outcomes assess downstream interaction under corrected pathology and MRI evidence on these 25 selected cases.

Answer-option sensitivity.

Physician review identifies 71 MCQ/very-short-answer pairs with the same target knowledge. Table A28 reports the number correct under each format and the paired difference. This control measures sensitivity to answer options while holding the knowledge target fixed.

MRI presentation.

The matched comparison evaluates Qwen3-VL-8B on 25 patients using a static panel, cine composed of the same frames, and an exploratory full-sequence cine condition. T accuracy is 32% in each condition. Same-frame cine minus static accuracy is 0.0 pp (95% CI: −16.0-16.0 to 16.0), comprising two wrong-to-right and two right-to-wrong changes. Structure-label micro accuracy changes by 1.3 pp (−9.6-9.6 to 11.8). Full-sequence cine changes T accuracy by 0.0 pp and structure accuracy by 2.2 pp (−7.3-7.3 to 11.1). The wide intervals leave substantial uncertainty about interface effects. A separate 11-model cine panel evaluates 2,700 card-matched tasks, 200 sequence tasks, and 100 patient-level tasks per model. The supplementary cine dataset provides the videos and their frame correspondence. Primary scoring reports card, sequence, and T-stage accuracy, while auxiliary scoring reports structure and invasion measures. This panel describes cine performance across additional models; the paired static/cine inference rests on the 25-patient comparison above.

C.5 Consultation Scoring and Results

O1 evaluates 103 consultation responses from each model against 1,726 clinician-defined criteria. Positive requirements measure what an answer should contain; error criteria identify claims or recommendations that warrant deductions.

C.5.1 Scoring Protocol

Table  reports the primary O1 ConsultRubrics results. Each model first generates one free-text consultation response for each of the 103 O1 items. Each response is assessed against its item-specific criteria, yielding 1,726 binary criterion judgments per model. For item ii, let 𝒜i\mathcal{A}_{i}, ℰimaj\mathcal{E}_{i}^{\mathrm{maj}}, and ℰimin\mathcal{E}_{i}^{\mathrm{min}} be the disjoint sets of positive requirements, major-error criteria, and minor-error criteria. Criterion kk has a binary judgment zi​k∈{0,1}z_{ik}\in\{0,1\}, corresponding to criteria_met. A positive-criterion judgment of one means the requirement is satisfied; a negative-criterion judgment of one means the error is present. Each positive anchor has clinician-assigned weight wi​k≥0w_{ik}\geq 0 in points. The available positive score is Bi=∑k∈𝒜iwi​k=10B_{i}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{A}_{i}}w_{ik}=10 points for every item.

Each triggered major error deducts two points, and each minor error deducts one point. The raw score rir_{i}, normalized score RiR_{i}, and primary model score are

ri\displaystyle r_{i} =max⁡{0,∑k∈𝒜iwi​k​zi​k−2​∑k∈ℰimajzi​k−∑k∈ℰiminzi​k},\displaystyle=\max\left\{0,\ \sum_{k\in\mathcal{A}_{i}}w_{ik}z_{ik}-2\sum_{k\in\mathcal{E}_{i}^{\mathrm{maj}}}z_{ik}-\sum_{k\in\mathcal{E}_{i}^{\mathrm{min}}}z_{ik}\right\}, (A7)
Ri\displaystyle R_{i} =100riBi,O1=1|𝒱|∑i∈𝒱Ri.\displaystyle=100\,\frac{r_{i}}{B_{i}},\qquad\mathrm{O1}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{V}}R_{i}.

Here 𝒱\mathcal{V} contains items with valid judgments for every criterion. Thus ri∈[0,10]r_{i}\in[0,10] is measured in points, while RiR_{i} and O1 lie in [0,100][0,100]. Deductions accumulate across criteria before the item score is floored at zero. The primary mean weights items equally; a clinical-tag score restricts 𝒱\mathcal{V} to items with that tag. All 30 generators have valid judgments for all 103 items, so |𝒱|=103|\mathcal{V}|=103.

Error rates have a different unit from score deductions. For severity s∈{maj,min}s\in\{\mathrm{maj},\mathrm{min}\}, let His=∑k∈ℰiszi​kH_{i}^{s}=\sum_{k\in\mathcal{E}_{i}^{s}}z_{ik} count triggered criteria. The item-level error rate is

ErrorRates=100|𝒱|∑i∈𝒱𝟏{His>0}.\mathrm{ErrorRate}_{s}=\frac{100}{|\mathcal{V}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{V}}\mathbf{1}\{H_{i}^{s}>0\}. (A8)

An item with several errors of the same severity contributes once to this percentage, although each error contributes its deduction in Eq. (A7). Figure 5d instead uses criteria as the unit: positive-section rates are the percentage of criteria satisfied, and error-avoidance rates are the percentage of error criteria not triggered. Each criterion counts once in that panel; clinician-assigned weights enter the consultation score in Eq. (A7). In panel (a), rr denotes the Pearson correlation across models between major-error rate and O1 score.

The primary judge is GPT-OSS-120B with greedy decoding and medium reasoning effort. Its criterion-specific prompt is shown in appendix E. All 30 generators use this same judge and scoring rule. Physician calibration separately assesses four judges on shared response–criterion pairs, as described in Appendix D.

C.5.2 Consultation Scores and Clinical Groups

Table  reports the score and the fraction of responses triggering each error severity. GPT-5.1 has the highest mean score, 58.4, but still triggers a major-error criterion in 14.6% of responses. Thus a higher score indicates better coverage and fewer deductions on average, rather than uniformly reliable clinical advice.

The 103 questions belong to 42 cases. The primary mean weights questions equally. Averaging first within each case and then across cases changes model scores by −2.0-2.0 to +0.1+0.1 points and leaves GPT-5.1 highest, as shown in Figure 5b. This comparison shows how the unequal number of questions per case affects the aggregate score.

Table A29 separates adverse-event management, diagnosis, treatment selection, special populations, and workup. Elderly and pediatric cases are reported separately here and combined in Figure 2h. Group sizes range from two workup questions to 43 treatment questions; these scores describe the included clinical questions rather than equally precise estimates for each area.

Appendix D Clinical Review and Judge Calibration

NPC specialists reviewed each item’s clinical question, available evidence, reference answer, and scoring criteria. They checked staging, prior treatment, toxicity, organ function, and guideline assumptions, and standardized drug names, doses, units, and answer options. Future orders and outcomes were removed from inputs when they disclosed the target decision. Question-review outcomes and the six unscored CarePath cohort treatment questions appear in appendices A and C.3.5.

D.1 Clinical Annotation and Adjudication

In routine care, pathology and radiology examinations were initially interpreted by a physician with 1–3 years of experience and finalized by a senior subspecialist with more than five years of experience. Pathology reference labels were taken from finalized reports. For benchmark MRI annotation, another physician independently reviewed the examinations, reports, and staging criteria to assign structure-invasion and T-category labels. Three senior NPC radiation oncologists resolved disagreements by consensus. The independent benchmark review followed routine clinical reporting and preceded consensus adjudication.

Review of clinical decisions.

For L2, reviewers checked whether the vignette supplied the facts needed for one guideline decision and whether the answer options supported a determinate choice. Missing variables, leading wording, and inconsistent guideline editions prompted revision. For L4, they assessed whether diagnosis, stage, treatment history, response, and contraindications supported the proposed management plan. The evaluated questions distinguish single-choice and explicit multiple-select items (appendix A).

For L5, review preserved the order of clinical events after date normalization and restricted each question to evidence available at that checkpoint. Distractors differed in evidence use, treatment timing, toxicity management, or follow-up requirements. For O1, specialists separated essential conclusions, supporting case evidence, and conditional recommendations, then assigned major and minor error penalties according to clinical severity.

D.2 Physician Calibration Audits

Targeted Audit.

For the automated O1 rubric judge, we constructed the Targeted Audit at the same criterion level as the scorer. The packet contained 811 criterion-level labels from 48 model-generated responses and was stratified to cover high judge disagreement, large score gaps, clinically safety-sensitive tags, and control cases with expected high or low rubric satisfaction. The physician worksheet marked responses whose completeness required review. Seventeen marked Gemini responses, comprising 263 criterion labels, were excluded because severe truncation prevented adjudication. Marked GPT-5.1 and GPT-OSS-120B responses remained eligible after physician confirmation that their individual criteria could still be judged. This left 548 criterion-level labels for the Targeted Audit agreement analysis. The retained set covers GPT-5.1, Qwen3.6-27B-Instruct, GPT-OSS-120B, and Gemini-3.1-Pro-Preview responses, allowing calibration across both API and local response generators. The 548 labels include 286 from marked responses: 184 GPT-5.1 and 102 GPT-OSS-120B labels. Excluding these responses leaves 262 labels for a sensitivity analysis, which gives the same judge ranking. The Expanded Audit broadens response-generator coverage, as described below.

Qwen3.6-27B criterion judging uses non-thinking mode, temperature 0, top-pp 1, and a 768-token output limit. Outputs missing required fields are retried up to four times; three remaining Targeted Audit judgments use JSON-schema-constrained decoding with the same prompts and model.

Expanded Audit.

Physicians annotated 1,017 criteria from 54 responses generated by nine models on six cases: 859 labels were collected with generator identity hidden and 158 came from the Targeted Audit. Comparisons use the 1,013 criteria judged by all four models; four criteria without a Qwen3.6-27B judgment are excluded from every judge’s comparison. Agreement is 77.6% for GPT-4.1, 70.5% for GPT-OSS-120B, 76.9% for Qwen3-30B, and 77.8% for Qwen3.6-27B, with Cohen’s κ\kappa of 0.547, 0.387, 0.538, and 0.544. The Targeted Audit (548 labels) and Expanded Audit (1,013 labels) are analysed separately because their response compositions differ. The primary O1 judge uses a criterion-specific template with four calibration examples and explicit interpretation of requirements and errors.

D.3 Agreement Measures and Sensitivity Analyses

Within either calibration set, let hℓ,h^ℓ∈{0,1}h_{\ell},\hat{h}_{\ell}\in\{0,1\} be the physician and judge labels for criterion ℓ\ell, and let nn be the number of valid paired labels. Define TP\mathrm{TP}, FP\mathrm{FP}, TN\mathrm{TN}, and FN\mathrm{FN} as the counts of (hℓ,h^ℓ)=(1,1),(0,1),(0,0),(1,0)(h_{\ell},\hat{h}_{\ell})=(1,1),(0,1),(0,0),(1,0), respectively; they sum to nn. A physician-positive label means the criterion is true. For a negative error criterion, this means an error is present, not that the response is clinically correct.

Observed agreement pop_{o}, physician-positive rate qHq_{H}, judge-positive rate qJq_{J}, chance agreement pep_{e}, and Cohen’s κ\kappa are

po=TP+TNn,qH=TP+FNn,qJ=TP+FPn,pe=qHqJ+(1−qH)(1−qJ),κ=po−pe1−pe.\begin{gathered}p_{o}=\frac{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{TN}}{n},\qquad q_{H}=\frac{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN}}{n},\qquad q_{J}=\frac{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}}{n},\\ p_{e}=q_{H}q_{J}+(1-q_{H})(1-q_{J}),\qquad\kappa=\frac{p_{o}-p_{e}}{1-p_{e}}.\end{gathered} (A9)

Sensitivity is TP/(TP+FN)\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN}), specificity is TN/(TN+FP)\mathrm{TN}/(\mathrm{TN}+\mathrm{FP}), and balanced agreement is their arithmetic mean. The first conditions on physician-positive labels and the second on physician-negative labels. These rates and pop_{o} are proportions; percentage agreement is 100​po100p_{o}, as in Table 2. The 262-label sensitivity table reports these measures as proportions, with True rate equal to qJq_{J}. Cohen’s κ\kappa is dimensionless. Each audit is evaluated separately.

Agreement by criterion type.

Figure 7e,j compares four judges with the 1,013 physician labels in the Expanded Audit, from 54 responses: nine generators each answer six cases. Sensitivity and specificity condition on physician-positive (n=456n=456) and physician-negative (n=557n=557) labels. Type-specific agreement counts matching binary judgments among 599 positive requirements, 225 major-error criteria, or 189 minor-error criteria. The positive requirements comprise core answers, key evidence, and conditional modifiers. These measures describe criterion recognition within consultations.

The figure’s intervals resample 54 complete response clusters, retaining all criteria within each response. We use the same 10,000 draws for every judge and endpoint (seed 20261029), with the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles as interval bounds. These responses share six case inputs, so a separate case-level analysis below retains all nine generators when resampling a case. The two analyses quantify variation between responses and between cases.

Table A32 reports the case-level resampling analysis and a leave-one-case-out check. The former retains all nine generators and every criterion for each sampled case; the latter examines whether agreement depends strongly on one case. These checks quantify sensitivity to the six cases represented in the Expanded Audit.

E.4 Consultation Generation and Judging

The response model sees the case and question. The judge additionally sees the generated answer and one signed criterion. A true judgment earns credit for a positive requirement and incurs a deduction for a negative error criterion.
